title: Love’s Labour’s Lost
author: William Shakespeare
setting: The King of Navarre’s park, and the field outside his gates where the French embassy is made to camp, over about two days
lengthNote: About 2,800 lines. Act V Scene 2 takes up some 900 of them, the longest scene in Shakespeare, and Berowne speaks more than anyone else in the play
openingLine: Let fame, that all hunt after in their lives,
summary: Four men swear off women, food and sleep for three years, and break the oath within a day of four women arriving on state business. What follows is made almost entirely of language: sonnets read aloud in a park while three men hide in the bushes, two letters delivered to the wrong hands, a schoolmaster’s Latin, a Spaniard’s prose, a masque of counterfeit Russians. The women win every exchange, and when a messenger brings news of a death in the last minutes they set the men a year of waiting instead of marrying them. It is the only Shakespeare comedy that ends with nobody married.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: This is the text the quotations were checked against, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, which modern editions vary from by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The verse and the rhyming put it beside A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Romeo and Juliet; no record fixes a first performance.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by William White for Cuthbert Burby, its title page naming Shakespeare and a performance before the Queen the previous Christmas.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: The names come from the French civil wars, the shapes from the academy, the embassy, the masque and the Nine Worthies pageant.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Seven of them are short. Act IV Scene 3 and Act V Scene 2 hold almost half the play between them.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: An oath signed, and broken by the next scene
structure.summary: Navarre and three friends sign a three-year statute against sleep, food and the sight of women. Berowne objects to every clause, points out that a French embassy is already on its way, and signs anyway. Within minutes Costard is arrested for being taken with Jaquenetta, and Armado, who reported him, admits he wants her himself.

scenes.title: The schedule
scenes.summary: The King reads out the rules of his academy; Berowne argues against study, signs, and hears the first case brought under the new law.

scenes.title: Armado in love
scenes.summary: Armado spars with his page Moth, is given Costard to keep, meets Jaquenetta in nine words, and resolves to write a sonnet.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The embassy is lodged in a field
structure.summary: The Princess of France arrives to settle a debt of a hundred thousand crowns and the ownership of Aquitaine. Navarre will not let her through the gate, so she negotiates standing outside it. Each of the four men picks out one of the four women and goes to Boyet afterwards to ask her name, which tells the audience how much attention the courtship has had.

scenes.title: Outside the gates
scenes.summary: Boyet flatters, the Princess refuses the flattery, the Aquitaine accounts are disputed and adjourned, and four men leave in love with four women they cannot name.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Two letters, one messenger
structure.summary: Armado sends Costard with a letter for Jaquenetta. Berowne, five minutes later, sends the same man with a poem for Rosaline. Nobody checks. The scene ends with Berowne alone, working out in fifty lines of self-disgust how a man who spent Act I mocking lovers has become one, and deciding to write anyway.

scenes.title: Remuneration and guerdon
scenes.summary: Moth and Armado play with words until Costard is freed and hired twice over; Berowne admits he is in love and curses Cupid at length.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Everything read aloud to the wrong person
structure.summary: The Princess hunts a deer and is handed Armado’s letter by mistake. Holofernes and Nathaniel are handed Berowne’s and send it straight to the King. Then, in the park, each of the four men in turn reads his own love poem out loud while the others listen from hiding, and Berowne, caught last, argues the oath away for all of them.

scenes.title: The hunt
scenes.summary: The Princess shoots for praise and knows it; Costard delivers Armado’s letter to her instead of Jaquenetta, and Boyet reads it out.

scenes.title: The schoolmaster
scenes.summary: Holofernes praises the deer in Latin and English, extemporises a poem on the letter L, and reads Berowne’s sonnet well enough to know it must go to the King.

scenes.title: The overhearing
scenes.summary: King, Longaville and Dumaine each read a sonnet aloud and each is overheard; Berowne mocks all three, is exposed by his own torn letter, and turns the oath inside out.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: A masque, a pageant, and a messenger
structure.summary: Holofernes casts the Nine Worthies. Warned in advance by Boyet, the women mask and swap the men’s gifts so that every disguised Russian courts the wrong woman. The pageant is heckled to a standstill, Costard announces Jaquenetta is pregnant, and Marcadé arrives with news that the Princess’s father is dead. The women leave, setting each man a year’s task.

scenes.title: Casting the Worthies
scenes.summary: Holofernes, Nathaniel, Armado, Moth, Costard and Dull agree on an entertainment, with the page complaining that the learned men eat words.

scenes.title: Favours, Worthies, Marcadé
scenes.summary: The women exchange tokens and wreck the Muscovite masque; the pageant collapses under heckling; death arrives; four proposals are deferred for a twelvemonth, and two songs close the play.

characters.name: Berowne
characters.role: The lord who argues against the oath, signs it, and breaks it first
characters.summary: He sees through the academy in Act I, lists everything wrong with it, and puts his name to the schedule anyway. His wit is the fastest on stage and he uses it on everyone, including himself, which is why the play gives him the longest speech in its defence of love and then makes him renounce that style completely in Act V.
characters.clue: The only man who argues against the oath before signing it, and the only one sentenced to a year in a hospital.

relationships.label: in love with, and judged by

characters.name: Rosaline
characters.role: The lady who matches Berowne line for line and sets his penance
characters.summary: She beats him in their first exchange in Act II before either has been introduced, leads the counter-masque in Act V, and ends by sending him to a hospital for a year to make the dying laugh. She is the one character who says plainly what a jest is worth and who decides it, and her judgement closes the play’s argument about wit.
characters.clue: She dances with him in Brabant before the play begins, and sends him to the speechless sick after it ends.

relationships.label: wooed by mistake in the masque

characters.name: The King of Navarre
characters.role: Founder of the academy, also called Ferdinand
characters.summary: He writes a three-year statute, suspends it within an hour for a visiting princess, and is the first of the four to be overheard reading a love poem. He wants Navarre to be the wonder of the world and keeps choosing the version of the rule that suits the moment. At the end he is sent to a hermitage to live the withdrawal he had planned as a route to fame.
characters.clue: The man who invented the rule he breaks first, and who is ordered to keep it alone for a year.

characters.name: The Princess of France
characters.role: Ambassador for her father, and queen before the play ends
characters.summary: She comes to recover Aquitaine and a hundred thousand crowns, is refused entry, and conducts the business from a tent. She refuses Boyet’s flattery in her first speech and knows exactly what her own deer-shooting is worth. When Marcadé arrives she becomes a queen in mourning, and she is the one who fixes the terms on which any of the four courtships may continue.
characters.clue: She is kept outside the gate for the whole play and is the only person in it with state business to finish.

relationships.label: kept outside his gates by, then courted
lets his pageant go on, over the King’s objection

characters.name: Boyet
characters.role: The lord attending the Princess, and the play’s best reader of faces
characters.summary: He flatters in his first speech and is told to stop. Afterwards he reads Navarre’s infatuation off the King’s own eyes and reports it, overhears the Muscovite rehearsal from behind a thicket and warns the women, then heckles the Nine Worthies. Berowne calls him a pedlar of wit and blames him for wrecking the masque, which is exactly what he did.
characters.clue: He hides under a sycamore, hears the whole plan and tells the women before the maskers arrive.

relationships.label: puts out of his part as herald of the masque

characters.name: Don Adriano de Armado
characters.role: A Spanish gentleman kept at court for entertainment
characters.summary: He reports Costard for being taken with Jaquenetta and is in love with her himself by the end of the scene. His prose is the most elaborate in the play, arranged in clauses that turn a walk in the park into a military dispatch. By Act V he has no shirt, a challenge on his hands, and a vow to hold the plough for Jaquenetta for three years.
characters.clue: He writes the letter that condemns Costard for the offence he is committing himself.

relationships.label: in love with, and the father of her child
reports, then jailer of, then challenged by

characters.name: Moth
characters.role: Armado’s page, and the fastest wit in the subplot
characters.summary: He takes his master apart in every exchange they have, proves that three years of study can be done in two words, and is the one who says what the learned men are doing with language when he calls it a feast whose scraps they have stolen. Cast as Hercules in minority, he is sent on to strangle a snake and sent off again before he can speak.
characters.clue: A page small enough to play Hercules as a baby, who out-argues everyone who owns him.

relationships.label: coached by, as herald of the masque

characters.name: Costard
characters.role: A countryman arrested in the first scene for keeping company with Jaquenetta
characters.summary: He is the first person punished under the new statute and the only character employed by both plots, carrying Armado’s letter and Berowne’s poem and mixing them up. He treats every word he is given as a coin to be valued, and in the last scene he is the one who tells the court that Jaquenetta is pregnant, which stops the pageant dead.
characters.clue: He is paid a remuneration by one master and a guerdon by the next, and prices both.

relationships.label: reported and jailed by, then challenges
shares the pageant and the jokes with

characters.name: Holofernes
characters.role: A schoolmaster who corrects everyone’s Latin
characters.summary: He describes a dead deer in four languages, writes a poem built on the letter L, and objects to people who say ‘dout’ without the b. He is ridiculous, and he is also the only man in the play who reads Berowne’s sonnet properly and sends it where it belongs. The lords bait him out of the pageant, and his exit line is the plainest complaint in the play.
characters.clue: He casts himself as three of the Nine Worthies and is heckled off the stage as Judas.

relationships.label: sends to the King with Berowne’s letter
casts in the pageant, and privately calls fantastical

characters.name: Jaquenetta
characters.role: A countrywoman, and the cause of the first arrest
characters.summary: She has fewer than twenty lines and sets most of the plot moving. Costard is jailed for being seen with her, Armado falls for her in one exchange of nine short answers, and she carries Berowne’s misdirected sonnet to the schoolmaster, who sends it to the King. In the last scene Costard announces she is two months pregnant, and Armado vows three years at the plough.
characters.clue: Nine flat answers to Armado in Act I, and a pregnancy announced in the middle of the Nine Worthies.

relationships.label: loved by, and bound to at the end
sent by, to carry the letter to the King

themes.name: Words as property
themes.summary: Everyone in the play treats words as things they own and can spend. Costard prices remuneration at three farthings and guerdon at elevenpence farthing. Holofernes hoards Latin, Armado hoards clauses, Nathaniel copies good phrases into a notebook, and Moth says the learned men have been at a feast of languages and stolen the scraps.
themes.development: In Act I the men sign away three years for the fame of having studied. By Act V Berowne swears off taffeta phrases and promises russet yeas and honest kersey noes, and the last thing the play offers is two songs about cuckoos, frozen milk and a greasy kitchen maid.

themes.name: Persuasion and proof
themes.summary: Berowne can argue any case. He argues against study and signs the schedule, argues that necessity excuses perjury, then argues in a hundred lines that love is the only real learning and that breaking the oath is a religious duty. Nobody on stage answers the argument; the women simply decline to act on it.
themes.development: The men’s case gets better and better and persuades nobody who matters. The Princess answers it once, in Act V, by saying that four hours of courtship is too short a time to make a world-without-end bargain in, and the argument stops there.

themes.name: Study and what it is for
themes.summary: The academy is founded to make Navarre the wonder of the world, with fame as the stated prize. Berowne’s objection in Act I is that plodders win nothing except the right to quote other men’s books, and that giving a name to every fixed star is not the same as knowing anything.
themes.development: Berowne replaces the library with women’s eyes and calls them the books, the arts, the academes. The ending replaces both: a hermitage for the King, a hospital ward for Berowne, and a year of silence for men who wanted three years of reading.

themes.name: Courtship as a show
themes.summary: Each of the four men produces a sonnet, reads it aloud, and is overheard. Then all four put on Russian costume and send a boy ahead with a prepared speech. The women watch the rehearsal reported by Boyet before they see the performance, and they know it is a performance before a word is spoken.
themes.development: The masque fails because the women swap favours and each man courts the wrong woman, proving that the show never depended on who was inside it. When the men return as themselves the Princess asks for confession, and after Marcadé the performing stops for good.

themes.name: Who is allowed to judge
themes.summary: The women are lodged in a field and have the better position from the start. The Princess refuses Boyet’s flattery in her first speech, catches the King out on the Aquitaine accounts, and directs the counter-masque. Rosaline names what a jest is worth and to whom, and sets the terms Berowne must meet.
themes.development: In Act II the women are the objects of four sonnets. In Act V they are the ones handing out sentences: a hermitage, a hospital, a twelvemonth and a day. The play’s last judgement on every male performance in it is delivered by the four people it was aimed at.

themes.name: What the oath was against
themes.summary: The statute forbids women, and desire is already inside the gates when it is signed. Costard is arrested in the first scene for being taken with Jaquenetta; Armado, who reported him, is in love with her himself by the end of the second; and Berowne is writing sonnets before the third act is over.
themes.development: Desire starts as a legal offence with a penalty attached and ends as a pregnancy announced in the middle of a pageant. Armado’s vow to hold the plough for Jaquenetta for three years is the only promise in the play that anybody is actually keeping when the curtain falls.

themes.name: A twelvemonth and a day
themes.summary: The play measures everything. Three years of study, a hundred thousand crowns, a year’s imprisonment for Costard, three farthings for a word, four hours of courtship. The Princess is the one who notices that the courtships have had no time in them at all, and who supplies the missing year.
themes.development: The men set a three-year term in Act I and abandon it in Act IV. The women set a twelve-month term in Act V and leave to keep it. Berowne says a twelvemonth is too long for a play, which is the only complaint about the ending the play does not answer.

techniques.name: Punning
techniques.definition: Playing on a word’s second meaning so that two senses are live at once.
techniques.inThisBook: Light runs through Act V as brightness, weight and loose behaviour in the same exchange between Rosaline and Katharine. Holofernes builds a whole poem out of adding an L to sore. The play has more puns than anything else Shakespeare wrote, and most of them are in the mouths of people trying to win.

techniques.name: Sonnets inside the play
techniques.definition: A complete fourteen-line poem set into the dialogue and spoken as a written object.
techniques.inThisBook: Four of them are read aloud: Berowne’s to Rosaline in Act IV Scene 2, then the King’s, Longaville’s and Dumaine’s in the overhearing scene. Each is a competent example of the fashion. Hearing four in a row makes the fashion audible, and the feeling underneath it much harder to hear.

techniques.name: The two songs
techniques.definition: A sung passage set outside the dialogue, free to say what the speaking characters cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Spring and Winter close the play with cuckoo-buds, ploughmen’s clocks, frozen milk and a maid keeling a pot. Nothing in either song is courtly, and after five acts of taffeta phrases they are the first plain speech the audience hears from the stage.

techniques.name: The second court
techniques.definition: A second story running beside the first, repeating its problem in another key.
techniques.inThisBook: Armado, Moth, Costard, Jaquenetta, Holofernes and Nathaniel are doing what the lords are doing: writing letters, showing off learning, staging entertainments, falling in love against orders. The lords laugh at them for it in Act V, forty lines after being caught doing the same things themselves.

techniques.name: The Muscovite masque
techniques.definition: Characters concealing their identity, so that the audience knows more than the people on stage do.
techniques.inThisBook: The men arrive in Russian habit with a rehearsed speech. The women mask too and swap the gifts each man sent, so that every whispered vow lands on the wrong ear. The disguise fails twice over: the women know who is under it, and the men do not know who they are talking to.

techniques.name: The overhearing scene
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself.
techniques.inThisBook: Act IV Scene 3 stacks four men in one park. Berowne hides, the King comes in and reads, the King hides, Longaville comes in and reads, and so on, until Berowne steps out to whip hypocrisy and is exposed by his own torn letter. The structure is a machine, and every man in it thinks he is the audience.

techniques.name: One voice each
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.inThisBook: Armado writes in nested clauses that postpone the verb. Holofernes doubles every English word with its Latin twin. Costard hears words as coins. Moth answers in two-beat replies. Boyet can read a man’s face out loud. Any ten lines of the play names its speaker without a prefix.

quotations.text: Let fame, that all hunt after in their lives, Live registered upon our brazen tombs
quotations.speaker: King of Navarre
quotations.context: The first words of the play, opening the academy.
quotations.analysis: The academy is founded on an epitaph. Before any rule is read out, the King has imagined the tomb the studying is for, and the study itself is only the means. Berowne will spend eighty lines attacking exactly this, and the Princess will arrive in Act V in mourning for a father whose death makes all brazen tombs look different.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.1.1-2

quotations.text: Navarre shall be the wonder of the world; Our court shall be a little academe
quotations.speaker: King of Navarre
quotations.context: Setting out what the three years of study are meant to achieve.
quotations.analysis: Two claims in two lines, and they do not fit. A court that is to be the wonder of the world must be seen, and an academe shut against women and visitors cannot be. The contradiction is the plot: the first outsider to arrive is a princess on state business, and the gate has to open before the end of Act II.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.1.12-13

quotations.text: Small have continual plodders ever won, Save base authority from others’ books.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: Arguing against the academy, minutes before signing its statute.
quotations.analysis: The charge is that reading produces only the right to quote, and Berowne makes it in rhymed couplets of great polish, which is the joke the King catches at once: how well he is read, to reason against reading. The play keeps this shape throughout, giving its best arguments to people who are doing the opposite of what they say.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.1.86-87

quotations.text: Necessity will make us all forsworn Three thousand times within this three years’ space
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: Signing the schedule, after the King has already suspended one clause for the French embassy.
quotations.analysis: Berowne signs and predicts the failure in the same breath, which makes him honest and useless at once. Three thousand is a joke and also roughly right: every man on stage is forsworn within three acts. The play is more interested in what he does after being proved correct than in the prediction, and what he does is write a sonnet.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.1.149-150

quotations.text: I’ll lay my head to any good man’s hat These oaths and laws will prove an idle scorn.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: Alone with Costard after the King has sentenced him to bran and water.
quotations.analysis: The bet is laid in the same scene as the law, and Berowne wins it before the interval. What makes the line more than a joke is its placement: he says it while escorting the first man punished under the statute, so the audience hears the law’s collapse predicted over the head of the one person it has actually cost anything.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.1.274-275

quotations.text: Assist me, some extemporal god of rhyme, for I am sure I shall turn sonnet.
quotations.speaker: Don Adriano de Armado
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act I, having fallen for Jaquenetta.
quotations.analysis: Turn sonnet, as a man might turn Turk or turn soldier: love converts him into a literary form. Armado gets there three acts before the lords do, and his letter to Jaquenetta arrives in the Princess’s hands in Act IV while Berowne’s reaches a schoolmaster. The subplot is not imitating the main plot; it is ahead of it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 1.2.141-142

quotations.text: Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye, Not uttered by base sale of chapmen’s tongues.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: Her first speech, cutting off Boyet’s compliment.
quotations.analysis: She refuses the currency the play runs on before she has been on stage twenty lines, and she does it in the language of trade: beauty is not stock to be talked up by a pedlar. Everything the men do afterwards, from sonnets to the Muscovite masque, is base sale of chapmen’s tongues, and she has already declined to buy.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 2.1.15-16

quotations.text: ’Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord, And sin to break it.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: Standing outside the gates, told she cannot come in because of the vow.
quotations.analysis: She puts the men in a position they never work out of: the oath is wrong either way, so nothing they do about it can be virtuous. Berowne spends a hundred lines in Act IV arguing that breaking it is a religious duty, which is only half of what she said here, and she never grants him the other half.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 2.1.106-107

quotations.text: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Answering Berowne, who has just asked her the same question word for word.
quotations.analysis: She gives him his own sentence back unaltered, and it is the first thing she says to him. The tactic sets the pattern for every exchange they have: he supplies the material and she returns it with the ownership changed. It also tells the audience they have met before, so the courtship the men think they are starting is already several years old.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 2.1.116

quotations.text: Why, all his behaviours did make their retire To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire.
quotations.speaker: Boyet
quotations.context: Telling the Princess that Navarre has fallen for her.
quotations.analysis: Boyet reads a face the way the lords read books, and he is right. The pun on court does the work: the King’s whole household has withdrawn into one organ, so the academy has already shrunk to the size of a man looking at a woman. Berowne will build his Act IV defence of love out of eyes, and Boyet has got there first.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 2.1.241-242

quotations.text: “Remuneration”! O, that’s the Latin word for three farthings.
quotations.speaker: Costard
quotations.context: Alone, after Armado has paid him for carrying a letter.
quotations.analysis: He works out the exchange rate of a word by what it bought, which is the only honest method anyone in the play uses. Berowne pays him a guerdon eighty lines later and Costard prices that too, at elevenpence farthing better. Set beside Holofernes hoarding Latin for its own sake, the countryman’s accounting looks like the sane position.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 3.1.114-115

quotations.text: This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy, This Signior Junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: Alone, admitting he is in love and furious about it.
quotations.analysis: Four adjectives and then a title that contradicts itself twice over, junior and signior, giant and dwarf. Berowne abuses Cupid in the most elaborate style he has, which is the joke: the man complaining about love-rhymes is composing one. The speech ends with him agreeing to love, write, sigh, pray, sue and groan, in that order.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 3.1.152-153

quotations.text: Glory grows guilty of detested crimes, When, for fame’s sake, for praise, an outward part, We bend to that the working of the heart
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: About to shoot a deer she does not want to kill.
quotations.analysis: She is describing herself: she will shoot for the credit of shooting well. The lines put a name to what the King did in the play’s first speech, hunting fame and bending the heart to it, and they come from the only character who admits to doing it. Four scenes later the deer is dead and Holofernes has written a poem about it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 4.1.32-34

quotations.text: The preyful Princess pierced and pricked a pretty pleasing pricket
quotations.speaker: Holofernes
quotations.context: Improvising an epitaph on the deer for Sir Nathaniel.
quotations.analysis: Six words beginning with p, which Holofernes calls affecting the letter and says argues facility. It is a complete school exercise, executed correctly and for nothing. He follows it with a poem that gets fifty sores out of one by adding the letter L, and he is genuinely pleased. The scene is funny and also the clearest picture in the play of learning with no object.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 4.2.51

quotations.text: From women’s eyes this doctrine I derive. They sparkle still the right Promethean fire; They are the books, the arts, the academes, That show, contain, and nourish, all the world
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: All four men are now exposed, and Berowne has been asked to prove their loving lawful.
quotations.analysis: The academy is not abandoned but relocated, with women installed where the library used to be. It is a magnificent argument and it keeps the men exactly where they started, treating women as the means to something else. The Princess answers it in Act V by asking for a year, and none of these hundred lines is any use to Berowne then.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 4.3.332-335

quotations.text: Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves, Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: The end of the speech that releases all four men from the statute.
quotations.analysis: The couplet turns on one verb used twice, and the balance is so neat that nobody on stage looks for the hole in it. Berowne is arguing that a promise you regret was never binding, which is what he told the King in Act I as a joke. The women’s reply is to give the four men a promise with a year attached.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 4.3.343-344

quotations.text: They have been at a great feast of languages and stolen the scraps.
quotations.speaker: Moth
quotations.context: Aside to Costard, watching Armado and Holofernes greet each other in Latin.
quotations.analysis: A page says in one sentence what the play takes five acts to demonstrate. The insult is precise: the scraps are real food, taken from a real feast, but nobody at this table cooked anything. Costard extends it at once, saying they have lived long on the almsbasket of words, which makes the learned men beggars living on other people’s leftovers.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.1.30-31

quotations.text: That he should be my fool, and I his fate.
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Telling the other women what she would do to Berowne if she had him in her power.
quotations.analysis: Said as a fantasy of revenge, and by the end of the scene it has come true in a form she has not imagined: she does become his fate, and the sentence she passes is a year among the dying. The line is worth setting beside her last speech, where the same wit that plans this torture is used to explain what a jest costs.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.70

quotations.text: Henceforth my wooing mind shall be expressed In russet yeas and honest kersey noes.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: After the Muscovite masque has been exposed, renouncing taffeta phrases.
quotations.analysis: Russet and kersey are cheap cloth, set against the taffeta and three-piled hyperboles he has just forsworn, so the renunciation is still a figure of speech. Rosaline catches it two lines later when he says sans crack or flaw and she asks him to drop the sans. He admits he has a trick of the old rage and will leave it by degrees.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.435-436

quotations.text: I am sorry, madam, for the news I bring Is heavy in my tongue. The King your father—
quotations.speaker: Marcadé
quotations.context: Entering in the middle of the Nine Worthies, as Armado and Costard square up to fight.
quotations.analysis: He never finishes the sentence; the Princess does it for him. Two and a half lines of plain statement stop a scene that has run nearly seven hundred, and Berowne’s response is the stage direction in words: worthies away, the scene begins to cloud. Nothing said after this has the same footing as anything said before it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.718-719

quotations.text: A time, methinks, too short To make a world-without-end bargain in.
quotations.speaker: Princess of France
quotations.context: The King has asked, at the latest minute of the hour, for her love.
quotations.analysis: World-without-end comes from the prayer book, and she uses it to measure marriage against the few hours the courtship has actually lasted. This is the answer to everything Berowne argued in Act IV, and it is not a refusal: she sets a hermitage and a year, and says come challenge me by these deserts. The terms are the point.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.790-791

quotations.text: A jest’s prosperity lies in the ear Of him that hears it, never in the tongue Of him that makes it.
quotations.speaker: Rosaline
quotations.context: Explaining why Berowne must spend a year making the sick laugh.
quotations.analysis: The whole play is tested against this sentence. Every wit in it has assumed the credit belongs to the speaker, and Rosaline moves it to the listener. It also justifies her sentence exactly: if the dying will laugh at his jokes he may keep them, and if they will not, the fault was never in their ears.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.859-861

quotations.text: Our wooing doth not end like an old play. Jack hath not Jill.
quotations.speaker: Berowne
quotations.context: After all four women have set their terms and are leaving.
quotations.analysis: He names the genre the audience expected and says it has not arrived, and the King answers that it wants a twelvemonth and a day, to which Berowne replies that is too long for a play. Two characters stand inside the story and discuss its shape, and the ending they describe is the one they are in.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.872-873

quotations.text: When icicles hang by the wall, And Dick the shepherd blows his nail
quotations.speaker: Winter
quotations.context: The second of the two songs that close the play, sung by the pageant players.
quotations.analysis: Dick, Tom, Marian and greasy Joan are the first people in the play with ordinary names and ordinary jobs, and they arrive in the last ninety seconds. The song has no wit in it at all, only frozen milk, a red nose and a staring owl, and it is the plainest and best-liked writing in the whole comedy.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 100, Love’s Labour’s Lost 5.2.908-909

timeline.label: A French embassy visits the real Navarre
timeline.detail: Catherine de’ Medici and her daughter Marguerite de Valois travelled to Henri of Navarre’s court at Nérac with a train of ladies, to settle the terms of Marguerite’s dowry and the disputed lands of the south-west. The play’s situation is this visit with the politics kept and the outcome changed.

timeline.label: English troops fight beside Navarre’s commanders
timeline.detail: Essex took an English force to Normandy in support of Henri of Navarre. The Duc de Biron, the Duc de Longueville and the Duc de Mayenne were named in the newsbooks that came back, and Shakespeare gave three of them to the lords of the academy.

timeline.label: The play written
timeline.detail: The rhyming, the sonnets set into the dialogue and the density of the wordplay place it beside A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Romeo and Juliet in the middle of the 1590s. No document records a first performance.

timeline.label: Presented before the Queen at Christmas
timeline.detail: The title page of the following year’s quarto says the comedy was presented before her Highness the last Christmas, which puts a court performance in the holiday season of 1597 and 1598.

timeline.label: The first quarto printed
timeline.detail: William White printed it for the bookseller Cuthbert Burby, describing it as newly corrected and augmented, with Shakespeare’s name on the title page. It is the only substantive early text: the Folio was set from a copy of it.

timeline.label: Francis Meres names it
timeline.detail: Palladis Tamia lists Love’s Labour’s Lost among the comedies that show Shakespeare most excellent, alongside a title, Love’s Labour’s Won, that nobody has since identified.

timeline.label: Robert Tofte reports seeing it played
timeline.detail: The poem Alba: The Months Minde of a Melancholy Lover describes watching Love’s Labour’s Lost and finding the comedy painful to sit through as a man in love. It is the earliest response to a performance by anyone in the audience.

timeline.label: Revived for Queen Anne
timeline.detail: Sir Walter Cope wrote to Robert Cecil in January that Burbage knew of no new play the Queen had not seen, but that the company had revived an old one called Love’s Labour’s Lost, which for wit and mirth he thought would please her exceedingly.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: Heminges and Condell placed it among the comedies, in a text set from the 1598 quarto. The Folio keeps the quarto’s duplicated passages in Act IV and Act V, where an earlier and a revised version of the same speech both stand.

timeline.label: A second quarto
timeline.detail: John Smethwick published a fresh quarto, printed from the Folio text. After this the play disappears from the record of performance for two hundred years.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris revives it at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: The first recorded professional production since the reign of James I. It ran briefly and was not much liked, and the comedy kept its reputation as an early experiment too clever to play.

timeline.label: Peter Brook’s production at Stratford
timeline.detail: Brook set the play in the world of Watteau, with Paul Scofield as Armado, and made Marcadé’s entrance the hinge of the evening. The production is generally credited with returning the comedy to the regular repertory.

places.name: Nérac
places.note: Henri of Navarre’s court, where a French queen and her ladies came to negotiate in 1578 and were entertained in the park.

places.name: Pamplona
places.note: The old capital of Navarre, the kingdom the King rules and proposes to make the wonder of the world.

places.name: Bordeaux
places.note: In Aquitaine, the province held in surety for a hundred thousand crowns and argued over in Act II.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where a court performance at Christmas 1597 is most likely to have taken place, as the 1598 title page reports.

places.name: Cornhill, London
places.note: Cuthbert Burby kept his shop here and sold the first quarto in 1598.

places.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Peter Brook’s 1946 production here brought the comedy back into the repertory after a century of neglect.

criticalViews.position: A coterie play, written for people who were in on it
criticalViews.summary: The density of the wordplay, the jokes at the expense of pedants and Italianate travellers, and the names lifted from French court politics have long suggested a first audience of lawyers, courtiers or a private household who would catch every reference.
criticalViews.counter: Burby sold it publicly in 1598 and Robert Tofte saw it in a playhouse the same year. Most of the comedy that lands in performance is physical: four men hiding in a park, a pageant heckled to pieces, a boy who cannot get through his speech. None of that needs a glossary.

criticalViews.position: The women are the play’s intelligence
criticalViews.summary: The Princess and her ladies see through every male performance, control the counter-masque, and end by imposing terms. On this reading the comedy is about four men being taught that fluency is not evidence, with the teaching done entirely by the women.
criticalViews.counter: Rosaline sentences Berowne for a wit he has already renounced forty lines earlier, in the russet yeas speech, and the women join in the heckling of the Nine Worthies as readily as the men. Their judgement is better, but it is not disinterested.

criticalViews.position: The ending is a deliberate refusal of comic form
criticalViews.summary: Berowne says the wooing does not end like an old play, and the twelvemonth pushes every marriage past the last line. Read this way, the comedy is an early experiment in the unfinished ending, closer to Chekhov than to the plays around it.
criticalViews.counter: Meres lists a Love’s Labour’s Won in 1598, and a bookseller’s list of 1603 names it too. If a companion play existed, this ending may have been the interval of a pair, and the refusal we admire could be a hinge that lost its other half.

essayQuestions.question: How far does Love’s Labour’s Lost suggest that clever language and honest feeling are different things?
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, sincerity and the test the play applies to both
plan: Start with Berowne in Act I arguing brilliantly against study and signing the schedule anyway, so that the best argument in the scene changes nothing.
Set the four sonnets of Act IV Scene 3 side by side: each is competent, each uses the same eyes and suns, and hearing them together makes the feeling sound rented.
Use Armado and Holofernes to test whether difficulty is the real charge, since Moth calls both men scrap-eaters while speaking faster than either.
Weigh Berowne’s promise of russet yeas and honest kersey noes against Rosaline’s reply two lines later, where he admits he cannot drop the trick all at once.
Close on the Winter song, where Dick, Tom and greasy Joan arrive with no wit at all and the writing improves.

essayQuestions.question: Why does Shakespeare give the Princess and her ladies the last word on every courtship?
essayQuestions.focus: Judgement, evidence and the women’s position outside the gates
plan: Begin with the Princess refusing Boyet’s compliment in her first speech, which sets the standard she applies to everything afterwards.
Show her catching the King on the Aquitaine accounts in Act II, so that her authority is established as business before it becomes romantic.
Use the swapped favours in Act V: the masque fails because each man courts the wrong woman, which settles the question by experiment.
Examine the terms set at the end, noting that each one is fitted to the particular man, and that all four are accepted.
Ask what it costs the play to leave these judgements unanswered, since no male character disputes a single one of them.

essayQuestions.question: What does Marcadé’s entrance do to the four acts that come before it?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, tone and the effect of death on a comedy
plan: Fix the moment precisely: Armado has challenged Costard, the pageant is in ruins, and the news arrives with about a hundred and fifty lines of the play left.
Track what stops immediately, including the Worthies, the heckling, and Berowne’s habit of commenting on everything.
Look at Katharine’s account in Act V of a sister who died of love, which puts a death in the play long before the messenger does.
Compare the King’s laboured speech about the extreme parts of time with Berowne’s plainer one, and note which of them the Princess says she understands.
Decide whether the entrance changes what the earlier acts meant, or only how they now sound.

essayQuestions.question: Is the Nine Worthies pageant comedy at the expense of the lords or of the players?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, performance and who is being laughed at
plan: Set out who is on stage: a schoolmaster, a curate, a page, a countryman and a penniless Spaniard, performing for a court that has just been humiliated.
Note the timing, since the lords begin heckling less than a hundred lines after being exposed in Russian costume.
Use Holofernes’s exit line about the baiting not being generous, gentle or humble, and Costard’s defence of Nathaniel as a foolish mild man and a very good bowler.
Weigh the Princess’s intervention, where she overrules the King and lets the show go on because zeal striving to content is worth watching.
Consider how a production’s choice about the heckling’s cruelty changes the ending, since Armado and the players are the ones who sing the final songs.

discussionQuestions: Berowne lists everything wrong with the oath and then signs it. Why does he sign?
The Princess is kept outside the gates for the whole play and wins every exchange from there. What does the position give her?
Armado falls in love with Jaquenetta, gets her pregnant and vows three years at the plough. Is the subplot laughing at him or at the lords?
The Muscovite masque fails because the women swap favours. What does that prove about how well the men know the women they are courting?
Rosaline sends Berowne to make the dying laugh for a year. Is that a punishment, a test, or a job she thinks he can do?
The play ends with two songs about cuckoos and frozen milk. Why finish a comedy about brilliant talk with something this plain?

related.why: Beatrice and Benedick are Berowne and Rosaline given a second chance: the same sparring, the same overhearing in a garden, and a death that changes the tone of the last act.
Written within a year or two of it, and turning on the same joke of lovers who cannot tell each other apart, ending with a rustic pageant that an aristocratic audience talks over.
Another comedy where courtship happens away from the court and a woman sets the conditions, though Rosalind takes a year’s worth of testing and compresses it into a forest.
The four sonnets read aloud in Act IV are the fashion the sequence works in, and Berowne’s defence of a dark mistress against the King is the argument of the later sonnets in miniature.
The other English comedy made almost entirely of epigram, where every proposal is a performance and the plot turns on a misdirected document.
